data: This course offers an accessible introduction to political anthropology by tracing how the field emerged, how it relates to allied disciplines, and what makes anthropological approach to power and politics distinctive. Through close readings of foundational texts, key theoretical debates, and ethnographic case studies from diverse contexts, students will explore how political anthropology has evolved, what questions its practitioners grapple with today, and what the framework contributes—as well as where its limits lie—in understanding political life. Organized into five modules, the course examines the field’s origins and boundaries; anthropological perspectives on politics and the political; debates around the nation, state, public sphere, and civil society; anthropological approaches to protest and revolution; and ethnographies of political violence.
Assistant Professor, Sociology and Social Anthropology
